intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with variable intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies (DIDDF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the JARID2 gene (601594) on chromosome 6p22.3.

paragraphs.text: Developmental delay with variable intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies (DIDDF) is a neurodevelopmental disorder. Features include developmental delay, cognitive impairment ranging from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, autistic features, and behavioral abnormalities. Dysmorphic facial features include high anterior hairline, broad forehead, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, and full lips (summary by Verberne et al., 2022). Some patients have palatal abnormalities and heart defects, and expressivity is variable (Cadieux-Dion et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) summarized the clinical features of 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants, some of whom had been reported earlier. The group included a mother and her daughter (patients 7 and 6) who carried the same deletion. All 8 had developmental delay. Intellectual functioning ranged from normal (patient 6) through learning difficulties and borderline intellectual functioning (IQ 82) to mild intellectual disability and moderate intellectual disability. Two patients had a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, and others had autistic features or behavioral abnormalities. Hypotonia was present in 2 patients, and gait disturbance in 2. Brain MRI showed a small posterior fossa cyst or mega cisterna magna in 1 patient and an arachnoid cyst in another. Variable dysmorphic features included broad forehead, high anterior hairline, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, midface hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, short philtrum, and full lips. One patient had prominent supraorbital ridges. Other anomalies were seen in single patients: submucous cleft palate with bifid uvula, pes planovalgus, cryptorchidism, congenital torticollis, kyphoscoliosis, a supernumerary tooth, and cafe-au-lait macules.

paragraphs.text: Baroy et al. (2013) reported 5 unrelated patients with de novo deletions, 0.1 to 4.8 Mb in size, in chromosome 6p22.3-p24.1. The deletions were found by array CGH in a cohort of about 3,600 patients ascertained for neurodevelopmental disorders. Patients 4 and 5 had non-overlapping deletions, and both deletions lay within the deletions of patients 1 to 3. Patients 1 to 4 shared a smallest region of overlap (SRO I) of 189 kb, which contained the JARID2 and DTNBP1 genes. Patient 4 had a 189-kb deletion that removed exons 3 to 18 of JARID2 and exons 7 to 10 of DTNBP1. Patients 1 to 4 had variable cognitive impairment, ranging from borderline IQ (74 in patient 4) to severe intellectual disability. They also had gait disturbance and similar facial dysmorphism, including prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, dark infraorbital circles, and midface hypoplasia. Additional features were bulbous nasal tip, full lips, marked Cupid's bow, prominent or pointed chin, clinodactyly of the fifth fingers, and foot anomalies. Seizures occurred in 2 patients, an atrial septal defect in 1, and autism spectrum disorder in 1. JARID2 expression in leukocytes was significantly reduced in patients 1 to 4 compared with controls. Baroy et al. (2013) suggested that JARID2 haploinsufficiency might be a clinically recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome. On review of photographs of 7 of 10 previously reported patients with deletions including JARID2, they confirmed a similar facial pattern.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) studied 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants. Six had deletions of at least 1 exon of JARID2, 1 had a frameshift variant (c.2866dupG), and 1 had a splice site variant (c.2731+1G-C). Peripheral blood DNA methylation profiling found a specific episignature that clearly separated these patients from 56 controls and from patients with other neurodevelopmental disorders. Three patients carrying JARID2 missense variants of uncertain significance (E644K and R788Q) clustered with controls. The authors considered these missense variants possibly benign.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) reported a de novo heterozygous 1-bp duplication (c.2866dupG, NM_004973.4) in the JARID2 gene in a 14-year-old boy (patient 4) with developmental delay and moderate intellectual disability. The duplication was predicted to cause a frameshift (Glu956GlyfsTer72). He also had autism spectrum disorder, behavioral abnormalities, high anterior hairline, short philtrum, and full lips. The variant was classified as pathogenic. His blood DNA methylation profile matched the JARID2 episignature.

His blood DNA methylation profile matched the JARID2 episignature.
